To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a voluntary intake of a high fat diet (HFD) in male rats increases energy expenditure and enhances adiposity; 2) a HFD does not modify muscle and liver oxidative capacity in either gender; and 3) HFD feeding increases UCP1 and 3 protein levels in order to maintain the balance between energy intake and expenditure, thus counteracting the effects of the diet.

male and female rats fed a high fat diet for 14 weeks did not show any significant changes in oxidative metabolism or oxidative stress in muscle and liver, despite the fact that they showed different responses to the diet in terms of body weight, energy intake and energy efficiency.

a HFD intake leads to an increase in energy expenditure and to a decrease in body fat deposition, which is accompanied by the over-expression of uncoupling proteins, thus counteracting the alteration induced by the modification in macronutrient composition in the diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that allow the maintenance of energy balance when the macronutrient proportion in the diet changes.
the effects of an isocaloric HFD on oxidative metabolism in skeletal muscle and liver.
the effects of a HFD on the whole animal energy expenditure and the oxidative metabolism of skeletal muscle and liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HFD feeding in male rats increases energy intake and adiposity but does not affect oxidative metabolism and oxidative damage in either muscle or liver.
the gender-related differences in the metabolic response to a HFD are mainly related to the different energy efficiency of the two genders.
a high fat diet, even when consumed isocalorically, does not induce changes in muscle and liver mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and oxidative damage in male and female rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gender-dependent metabolic response to a HFD is mainly determined by the energy intake and the body weight gain, while tissue oxidative metabolism is not modified.
the gender-dependent response to an isocloric intake of a high fat diet is mainly related to energy balance and not to oxidative metabolism.

HFD feeding induces a gender-specific metabolic response in order to maintain body weight and energy expenditure, which is achieved by increasing energy efficiency in males and by increasing energy expenditure in females.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gender-dependent response in energy balance and oxidative metabolism to a HFD intake is not related to the oxidative status in muscle and liver.

the isocaloric intake in a HFD did not modify oxidative metabolism in skeletal muscle and liver, and that the expression of uncoupling proteins is a compensatory mechanism to maintain energy balance and to avoid oxidative damage in response to the HFD.
the gender-dependent response of skeletal muscle and liver oxidative pathways to an HFD is due to the higher energy efficiency in male compared to female rats.
